symptom: Porosity in welds (small cavities or holes in the bead)
question: What setup or technique factor is most likely the cause?

cause: Insufficient or incorrect shielding gas on gas-shielded MIG: the molten puddle is exposed to atmosphere, trapping nitrogen and oxygen in the bead.
fixes: Increase shielding gas flow to 20-30 SCFH (p. 20)
Check the regulator gauge and verify the cylinder valve is open
Inspect gas hose and torch O-rings for leaks; replace damaged seals
Confirm you are using the correct gas for the wire (e.g. C25 for solid-core mild steel, 100% argon for aluminum)
Shield the work area from drafts; do not weld in a strong cross-breeze

cause: Surface contamination — oil, paint, rust, mill scale, or moisture — burns out during welding and forms gas pockets in the bead.
fixes: Clean the workpiece down to bare metal with a wire brush or grinder
Wipe off oils, coatings, and other residues before welding
Use a wire feed and filler that the manufacturer recommends for your wire type
Store welding wire indoors to keep it dry

cause: Travel speed too inconsistent or contact-tip-to-work distance (CTWD) too long; the shielding gas or flux can't keep up with the puddle.
fixes: Maintain a steady travel speed across the joint
Reduce CTWD: hold the gun so the contact tip is 3/8" to 1/2" from the work
Use a stable two-hand grip or rest the gun hand on the work for steadiness

cause: Polarity reversed for the wire type. Solid-core gas-shielded MIG runs DCEP (electrode positive); flux-cored runs DCEN (electrode negative).
fixes: For solid-core MIG: ground clamp into the Negative (−) socket, wire-feed power cable into the Positive (+) socket (p. 14)
For flux-cored: ground clamp into the Positive (+) socket, wire-feed power cable into the Negative (−) socket (p. 13)
Verify the polarity diagram on the welder door matches your wire

symptom: Inadequate penetration (weld sits on top of the joint instead of fusing into it)
question: Which process are you using?

cause: Not enough heat or filler at the joint: amperage/voltage too low, wire-feed speed too slow, or travel speed too fast.
fixes: Increase output voltage or wire-feed speed
Slow the travel speed and ensure it stays steady
Maintain 1/2" or less contact-tip-to-work distance (CTWD)
Keep arc on leading edge of weld puddle and hold the MIG gun at the proper angle
Bevel thick workpieces and allow a small gap before welding to increase fusion area
Use additional weld passes for thicker material

cause: Stick current too low, arc length too long, or travel speed too fast for the rod and thickness.
fixes: Increase welding current (within the rod manufacturer's range)
Shorten arc length: keep the rod close to the work
Slow travel speed; let the rod and base metal fuse together
Keep the rod arc on the leading edge of the weld puddle
Use the correct rod diameter for the thickness — thinner rods for thin stock, thicker for heavy plate

cause: TIG amperage too low or torch travel too fast; tungsten arc not delivering enough heat to fuse the joint.
fixes: Increase amperage on the foot pedal or panel control
Slow travel speed and dwell briefly on the joint
Verify tungsten is sharp and sized correctly for the amperage
Reduce arc length: hold the tungsten closer to the work

symptom: Welder does not function when switched on
question: What is the LCD display doing?

options.label: LCD is on but the welder will not arc

cause: Internal thermal-protection device has tripped — the welder shuts down to prevent damage when its duty-cycle limit is exceeded.
fixes: Leave the Power Switch ON and let the cooling fan run; the welder automatically returns to service after cooling
Reduce duration or frequency of welding periods to stay within the rated duty cycle (p. 7 / p. 19)
Avoid welding heavy beads in long continuous runs at the rated max amperage

cause: The welder is not receiving mains power, or the supply circuit cannot deliver the required current.
fixes: Verify the unit is plugged in and the outlet is powered
Check the circuit breaker or GFCI for the outlet; reset if tripped
Confirm the outlet matches the welder's input plug (120 VAC 20 A or 240 VAC) and supplies the required amperage (p. 7 specifications)
If using an extension cord, make sure it is the proper gauge and length for the welder's input current
Press the Reset button on the back of the welder if a fault breaker has tripped

cause: Welder is powered but the trigger / electrode circuit isn't completing — bad trigger connection, missing ground clamp, or wrong mode for the connected lead.
fixes: Re-seat the gun-trigger / TIG-foot-pedal connector and tighten the lock ring
Confirm the ground clamp is firmly attached to clean bare metal on the workpiece
Verify the LCD process matches the cables you have connected (MIG vs TIG vs Stick)
Check that the input range you selected on screen is within the welder's specified range (p. 7)

symptom: Excessive spatter in welds (large grainy spatter beyond the small fine spatter that is normal)
question: Which process is producing the spatter?

cause: Wire-feed and voltage setup is out of balance, polarity is wrong, contact-tip-to-work distance is too long, or workpiece is dirty.
fixes: Clean the workpiece and welding wire down to bare metal; free it from oil, coatings, residues
Check polarity against the wire type (DCEP for solid-core, DCEN for flux-cored — p. 13/14)
Increase shielding gas flow on gas-shielded MIG (20-30 SCFH per p. 20)
Reduce wire-feed speed
Shorten contact-tip-to-work distance

cause: Workpiece or electrode contamination, or current too high for the rod and base metal.
fixes: Clean the workpiece down to bare metal; ensure rods are dry and uncontaminated
Use a rod appropriate for the base metal alloy
Reduce welding current if it is at the top of the rod's range
Maintain steady arc length
